VS.

full_judgment:
The aforesaid charge was read over and explained to the accused appellant who pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried. To prove the charge the prosecution examined six witnesses (P.W. 1,2,5,6,7 and 8) and tendered two witnesses (P.W.3 and P.W. 4) while the defence examined none. 

 26. The next important witness on whom the trial Court relied is P.W. 2 M.S. Molla and admittedly he is an officer of the Customs Department working at the Zia International Air Porl. He deposed that on 30.5.88 at 11 A.M: the baggage’s of the appellant were placed for examination at the crews counter and those were placed in presence of Safiar Rahman (who is a material witness and we draw adverse inference against the prosecution for withholding him without any reason) and at that time he went there and they demanded baggage declaration form from the crew. He further deposed that they found the echo lac bag rather heavy and on being suspicious they took the appellant to the room of the Deputy Collector of Customs in whose presence the Echolac bag was .searched and they found gold bars in the pocket of the bag. He further deposed that the search was conducted in presence of the Deputy Collector of Customs Mr. Shahjad. Hossain who is a material witness and for withholding whom without any reason we draw adverse inference against the prosecution. P.W. 2. M.S. Moll a further deposed that he himself prepared the seizure list where the appellant put his signature. Appellant wrote that the gold bars do nor belong to him and that he does not know who had kept them. He says that the appellant himself identified his baggage’s, But P.W. 6 Mannaf and P.W. 7 Soheli stated that the appellant stated that the bag docs not belong to him. It is the definite case of the prosecution that the accused appellant carried the gold in an echolac bag and those were re- covered from that bag by the customs officials P.Ws. 1 and 2. We have already found that the evidence of P.W. 1 in this respect is not believable. It is the defence case that echolac bag in which the gold bars were found does not belong to the appellant. We found from the evidence of P.W. 1 and 2 that when- ever a passenger or a crew carry any baggage, the airline officials place baggage tag with it. This is done to identify the baggage of a particular crew or the passenger. Admittedly in flight No. B.G. 042 there were 12/13 crews all of whom came from Dubai and their baggage’s were placed before the customs officials for checking. Toe prosecution in such circumstances must prove that an echolac bag was found with the baggage’s and the bag which contained the gold bars belonged to the appellant and unless this is proved and established the appellant cannot be convicted and sentenced. P.W. 1 during cross- examination admitted that it is common practice and known to every body that the baggage tags have two parts. One part remains attached to the baggage and the other one remains with the passenger or the crew and the baggage’s are delivered after comparing both the parts of the tag. This is the system every where and that was introduced for proper identification of the baggage. Here in the present case before us P.W. 1 admitted that the echo lac bag had a baggage tag. Even P.W. 2 who allegedly searched the baggage of the appellant admitted that the echo lac bag within  which the gold was found had a baggage tag. So the evidence of these two witnesses is to the effect that the echolac bag had a baggage tag and that the appellant was also searched and all his belongings were seized by seizure list Ext. 5. This seizure list contained 46 items but in those 46 items we find no baggage tag. Now if the echolac bag had a baggage tag and if that bag actually belonged to the appellant and if he himself produced bag before the Customs Officer for checking the other part of the tag must have been with him. The Customs Officer failed to seize that baggage tag or recover it from the appellant and send both the baggage tags along with the bag to the trial Court to prove that the bag which contained the gold actually belong to the appellant. When there is specific denial by the defence that seized echolacbag docs not belong to the appellant, the prosecution has got to produce both the tags to prove that the bag belonged to the appellant. Furthermore P.W. 1 who is the informant himself admitted that such ccholac bags are available in the market. In such circumstances it was the duty of the prosecution to prove that the seized echolac bag actually belonged to the appellant. But here the Customs officials though seized the en- tire contents of the bag and they also arrested the appellant they have not seized the baggage tag for connecting the accused appellant with the echo lac bag from which the gold bars were recovered. If it is a fact that the echolac bag belonged to the appellant and that it contained the baggage tag, the non-seizure of the baggage tag along with the echolac bag is a de- liberate act on the part of the Customs officer for keeping a gap in the continuity of events and that has been done with intention. Since tag or tags of the bag were seized, •the normal presumption is that there were no tags attached to the bag to show that the bag belonged to the appellant.We have already found that P.W. 1 gave contradictory statement and P.W. 2 who prepared the seizure list and who conducted the search has not seized the baggage tag to prove conclusively that the bag belonged to the appellant. This may have been done with ulterior motive. These witnesses failed to prove that the seized bag actually belonged to the appellant. 

 28. In such circumstances after consideration of the materials on record we hold that the prosecution failed to connect the appellant with seized echolac bag. As already stated, the seizure list Ext. 1 docs not indicate in any manner that the passport and other items which weredescribed in items 1-9 were, found inside that echolac bag. None of the prosecution witnesses also stated so. We are, therefore of the view that the allegation of the prosecution against the appellant that the bag from which 31 gold bars were recovered belonged to the appellant has not been proved beyond reasonable doubt. 

 31. The next important point that has been raised by the learned Advocate for the appellant is about the proceeding of the trial under section 156 of the Customs Act and section 25 of the Special Powers Act. He submits that the entire proceeding is vitiated due to the trial of the offence punishable under the Customs Act as well as the Special Powers Act. He argued that the offence punishable under section 156(8) of the Customs Act is a non-schedule offence and this cannot be tried by any tribunal constituted under the Special Powers Act along with any offence punishable under Special Powers Act. From the personal of the record it is found that the police after investigation submitted charge-sheet under section 156(8) of the Customs Act read with section 16 and 25B of the Special Powers Act and under section 8 (1) of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947 and as charge-sheet was submitted under the Special Powers Act the record was sent to the Tribunal who received the case record on 4.11.46 and on personal of the record and charge-sheet took cognizance of the case under section 156(8) read with sections 16/25B of the Special Powers Act and section 8 of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act and transferred the same to the trial Court for disposal. The trial Court then on 5.3.87 framed charge under section 156(8) of the Customs Act read with section 25B(1) of the Special Powers Act. The learned Advocate for the appellant submits that as offences punishable under section 156(8) of the Customs Act arc not triable before the Special Tribunal being a non schedule of-fence, the proceeding of the case is illegal and without jurisdiction. He submits that as proceeding has been vitiated by joint trial by the Tribunal under two provisions of law, one is not triable before that Tribunal. Admittedly .offence punishable under section 156(8) of the Customs Act is not triable under the Special Powers Act. It is a non-schedule offence and it has a separate forum. But the tribunal took cognizance under the Customs Act and also under the Special Powers Act and charge was also framed accordingly and the appellant also was convicted under these provisions. The learned Advocate for the appellant submits that the decision of this Court is that such a proceeding is illegal and it vitiated the trial and he placed reliance on the decision reported in 33 D.L.R. 203 (Tamiz Mia -Vs. Bangladesh) where it has been held that the Special Tribunal constituted under the Special Powers Act has an exclusive jurisdiction to try exclusively only such offences as are mentioned in the Schedule to the Special Powers Act, that means, offence which arc not included in the schedule to the Special Powers Act can not be tried by any Special Tribunal constituted under the Special Powers Act. It has also been held that joinder of scheduled and non-scheduled offences is illegal and the trial by the Special Tribunal for both the of-fences was also without any lawful authority. 

 32. The learned Advocate for the appellant then placed another decision reported in 35 D.L.R. 127 (Talukder A. Azia Vs.State) where it has been held that the cognizance of the offence in a case like the present one suffers from inherent initial illegality as the scheduled and non-scheduled offences were joined together to be tried by the Special Tribunal at one trial whereas the Tribunal was constituted to try case mentioned in the schedule of the Special Powers Act and not for offences under the ordinary penal laws of the land. It has also been held in that decision that joinder of Schedule offences and non-schedule offences was thus illegal and so also the cognizance, taken by the Special Tribunal of both schedule and non-schedule offences were without jurisdiction. 

 33. In the present case before us it is found from the perusal of the record that the Special Tribunal constituted under the Special Powers Act took cognizance of the offence under section 156(8) of the Customs Act and under section 8 of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act which arc non Schedule of-fences. The Tribunal also framed charge under sections 156(8) of the Customs Act and 25B of the Special Powers Act and the Additional Sessions Judge and Ex-Officio Special Tribunal also tried together scheduled and non-scheduled offences though offences punishable under the Customs Act are not triable under the Special Powers Act. Furthermore the trial Court also found the appellant guilty of the offence punishable under section 156 (8) of the Customs Act and also the Special Powers Act and he awarded the sentence. In view of the trend of the decisions of this court as mentioned above we are of the view that the joinder of scheduled and non-scheduled offences in the present case vitiated the entire proceeding. The learned Tribunal committed illegality i7S1 taking cognizance of the case and in framing the charge and convicting and sentencing the appellants and it requires interference. 

 35. Having considered the materials on record and the relevant laws we are of the view that the proceeding has been clearly vitiated for illegal joinder of schedule and non-scheduled offences in one trial and we also hold that the prosecution failed to prove beyond all reasonable doubts the bringing of gold bars by the appellant inside Bangladesh without any legal authority. Appellant's contention that the Echolac bag with all its contents and the 31 gold bars (310 tolas) do not belong to him has been sufficiently probable. The said 31 gold bars shall, therefore, remain confiscated to the State.
